questions.question: What does it mean for an element g to generate a group G?
options: Repeating g with the group operation reaches every element of G
The value g is larger than every other encoded group element
The element g has no inverse under the group operation
Hashing g produces a uniformly random element of G
questions.explanation: The generated subgroup <g> contains all repeated powers or sums of g. If <g> = G, then g generates G.

questions.question: In a multiplicative group, what is the identity element usually written as?
options: 0, because multiplication starts counting from zero
1, because multiplying by it leaves elements unchanged
-1, because it reverses every multiplication
The modulus, because all arithmetic is reduced by it
questions.explanation: The multiplicative identity is 1: for every element a, 1*a = a*1 = a.

questions.question: Which statement describes a cyclic group?
options: A group whose elements can all be reached by repeating one element
A group whose operation table must be sorted in increasing order
A group that has no identity element but still has inverses
A group that only exists when the modulus is a composite number
questions.explanation: A cyclic group has at least one generator g such that <g> is the entire group.

questions.question: In Z/6Z under addition, why is 2 not a generator?
options: It has no additive inverse modulo 6
Its repeated sums cycle through 0, 2, and 4 only
It is not a valid residue modulo 6
It makes addition modulo 6 non-associative
questions.explanation: The generated subgroup <2> is {0, 2, 4}, so it does not reach every residue modulo 6.

questions.question: In (Z/7Z)^*, the element 3 has order 6. What does that imply?
options: 3 is a generator of the whole multiplicative group modulo 7
3 is outside the multiplicative group modulo 7
3 has no multiplicative inverse modulo 7
3 generates only the identity element
questions.explanation: (Z/7Z)^* has six elements. If an element has order six, its powers reach the whole group.

questions.question: What is a primitive root modulo a prime p?
options: A generator of the multiplicative group (Z/pZ)^*
Any residue whose decimal representation starts with 1
A number that divides p without leaving a remainder
The additive identity of Z/pZ
questions.explanation: A primitive root modulo p is a generator of the nonzero residues under multiplication modulo p.

questions.question: Why is a small-order base dangerous in a Diffie-Hellman-like protocol?
options: It makes modular multiplication impossible to compute
It restricts public values to a short cycle, leaking information about secret exponents
It guarantees every secret exponent is a prime number
It prevents public keys from being represented as integers
questions.explanation: If the base has small order, g^x depends only on x modulo that small order. That leaks constraints on the secret.

questions.question: What does a brute-force discrete logarithm search do in a small generated subgroup?
options: It tries e, g, g^2, and so on until the target appears
It factors the modulus before checking whether the target is prime
It changes the group operation so every element becomes a generator
It hashes the target repeatedly until the identity disappears
questions.explanation: The brute-force attack walks the generated cycle and returns the exponent where the target first appears.
